questions.question: What is the Gradle Wrapper (gradlew) and why is it important?
questions.title: Gradle Wrapper (gradlew)
questions.direct_answer: The Gradle Wrapper is a script (gradlew / gradlew.bat) checked into the project that downloads and runs the exact Gradle version specified for the project — ensuring everyone and every CI server uses the same Gradle version without needing Gradle installed globally.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical Gradle knowledge — the wrapper is what you use when working with Gradle projects
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Installing Gradle globally and using 'gradle build' instead of './gradlew build' — risks version mismatches
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Maven has a similar concept: the Maven Wrapper (mvnw) introduced later

sections.title: The Gradle Wrapper: Version Consistency Without Global Installation
sections.content:
The **Gradle Wrapper** (gradlew) is a set of scripts and a small JAR file checked into your project's version control.

Think of it like a self-contained installer: when you run ./gradlew build (or gradlew.bat build on Windows), the script checks if the correct Gradle version is already downloaded, downloads it if needed, and then runs your build with that exact version. This solves the **version hell problem** — different developers and CI servers no longer need Gradle installed globally, and everyone automatically uses the same Gradle version the project was configured for. The wrapper configuration lives in gradle/wrapper/gradle-wrapper.properties, which specifies the exact Gradle version (e.g., distributionUrl=...gradle-8.5-bin.zip). This pattern is now so popular that Maven adopted it with the **Maven Wrapper** (mvnw) years later.

sections.content:

blue|How|~Self-installing|reads gradle-wrapper.properties|downloads the exact version|then runs the build

sections.title: Using the Gradle Wrapper in Practice
sections.content:
```bash
// gradle/wrapper/gradle-wrapper.properties
distributionBase=GRADLE_USER_HOME
distributionPath=wrapper/dists
distributionUrl=https\://services.gradle.org/distributions/gradle-8.5-bin.zip
zipStoreBase=GRADLE_USER_HOME
zipStorePath=wrapper/dists

// Running builds with the wrapper (Unix/Mac)
./gradlew clean build
./gradlew test --tests UserServiceTest
./gradlew bootRun

// On Windows
gradlew.bat clean build

// Upgrading the Gradle version for the project
./gradlew wrapper --gradle-version 8.6

// CI configuration (GitHub Actions example)
steps:
  - uses: actions/checkout@v3
  - name: Build with Gradle
    run: ./gradlew build  # No Gradle installation needed
```

sections.title: When and Why to Use the Gradle Wrapper
sections.content: **Use the wrapper for all Gradle projects** — it's Gradle's recommended approach and should be committed to version control (including the gradlew scripts and gradle/wrapper/ directory). The wrapper ensures **build reproducibility**: a build that works today will work the same way in six months because the Gradle version is locked. It eliminates the "works on my machine" problem where one developer has Gradle 7.6 installed and another has 8.5, leading to different build behavior. For **CI/CD pipelines**, the wrapper is essential — your Jenkins or GitHub Actions job doesn't need Gradle pre-installed; it just runs ./gradlew build. The only time you'd use a global Gradle installation is when creating a new project (gradle init), but even then you'd immediately generate the wrapper with gradle wrapper.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using 'gradle' instead of './gradlew'**: Freshers often install Gradle globally and type gradle build, which uses whatever version they installed, not the project's version. This breaks reproducibility.
- **Not committing wrapper files**: The gradlew script, gradlew.bat, and gradle/wrapper/ directory must be committed to Git. Some freshers add them to .gitignore thinking they're build artifacts.
- **Forgetting to set execute permissions**: On Unix systems, gradlew needs execute permission (chmod +x gradlew). If it's not set, teammates get "permission denied" errors when trying to build.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Purpose**: gradlew ensures everyone uses the same Gradle version without global installation
- **Scripts**: gradlew (Unix/Mac) and gradlew.bat (Windows) are checked into version control
- **Configuration**: gradle/wrapper/gradle-wrapper.properties specifies the exact Gradle version via distributionUrl
- **First run**: The wrapper downloads the specified Gradle version to ~/.gradle/wrapper/dists/ on first use
- **CI/CD friendly**: No need to install Gradle on build servers — the wrapper handles it
- **Version upgrade**: Run ./gradlew wrapper --gradle-version X.Y to update the project's Gradle version
- **Maven equivalent**: Maven adopted this pattern later as the Maven Wrapper (mvnw)

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The Gradle Wrapper is a script you check into your project that lets anyone build your code without installing Gradle globally. It's the gradlew file on Unix or gradlew.bat on Windows. When you run ./gradlew build, the script first checks if the right Gradle version is already downloaded. If not, it downloads it automatically, then runs your build. The version is specified in a properties file, so everyone on the team and every CI server uses the exact same Gradle version. This solves the version mismatch problem. If I have Gradle 7 installed and you have Gradle 8, we'd get different build results. With the wrapper, we both use whatever version the project says to use, say Gradle 8.5. You commit the wrapper files to Git — the gradlew scripts and the gradle wrapper directory. One common mistake freshers make is installing Gradle globally and typing gradle build instead of ./gradlew build. That defeats the whole purpose because you're using your globally installed version, not the project's version. Maven eventually copied this idea and created the Maven Wrapper, which works the same way.

questions.question: What are the key differences between Maven and Gradle?
questions.title: Maven vs Gradle: Key Differences
questions.direct_answer: Maven uses XML configuration (pom.xml) with a rigid convention-based lifecycle; Gradle uses a Groovy/Kotlin DSL with a flexible, programmatic build model and significantly faster incremental and cached builds.

interviewer_intent.testing: Informed comparison of the two dominant Java build tools — expect this question at mid-to-senior level interviews
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying one is universally better without acknowledging trade-offs and context
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention Gradle's build cache and incremental compilation as the key performance differentiators in large projects

sections.title: Maven vs Gradle: Two Approaches to Build Automation
sections.content:
**Maven** and **Gradle** are both build automation tools that manage dependencies, compile code, run tests, and package applications. Think of them like recipe books: Maven gives you a fixed recipe you must follow step-by-step (declarative XML), while Gradle gives you ingredients and techniques you can combine flexibly (imperative Groovy/Kotlin scripts). Maven's strength is **convention over configuration** — projects follow a standard structure (src/main/java, src/test/java) and a predictable lifecycle (compile → test → package).

This makes Maven builds easy to understand but hard to customize. Gradle's strength is **performance and flexibility** — it can express complex build logic naturally and uses incremental builds plus a build cache to avoid redundant work. In large projects with hundreds of modules, Gradle can be 10-100x faster than Maven for incremental builds.

sections.title: Maven: Declarative XML (pom.xml)
sections.content:
```xml
<!-- verbose but predictable -->
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
</dependency>
```

sections.title: Gradle: Concise DSL (build.gradle)
Maven vs Gradle: Key Differences
sections.content:
| Aspect | Maven | Gradle |
|---|---|---|
| Configuration | XML (pom.xml), declarative | Groovy/Kotlin DSL, programmatic |
| Build Speed | Slower, rebuilds more | Faster with incremental builds + cache |
| Flexibility | Rigid lifecycle, hard to customize | Highly flexible, easy custom tasks |
| Learning Curve | Easier for beginners | Steeper, requires DSL knowledge |
| Adoption | Dominant in enterprise Java | Growing, standard for Android |

sections.title: When to Choose Each Tool
sections.content: **Use Maven when** you want maximum compatibility and team familiarity — most Java developers know Maven, most open-source libraries document Maven coordinates, and enterprise teams often have Maven expertise. Maven's strict conventions make it harder to create non-standard builds, which can be an advantage for maintainability. **Use Gradle when** build performance matters (large multi-module projects), you need custom build logic (code generation, multi-platform builds), or you're building Android apps (Gradle is the only supported tool). Gradle's flexibility shines when you need to integrate non-Java tools or orchestrate complex workflows that don't fit Maven's rigid lifecycle.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Choosing based on hype**: Freshers often say "I'd use Gradle because it's modern" without considering that a team with zero Gradle experience will struggle with even simple customizations.
- **Not understanding the real speed difference**: Gradle isn't magically faster — it's faster for *incremental* builds when you change a few files, not clean builds from scratch.
- **Ignoring IDE support**: Both IntelliJ IDEA and Eclipse support Maven better than Gradle because Maven's been around longer; Gradle projects sometimes have IDE sync issues that waste time.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Configuration style**: Maven uses XML (pom.xml), Gradle uses Groovy or Kotlin DSL (build.gradle or build.gradle.kts)
- **Build performance**: Gradle's incremental builds and build cache make it significantly faster for large projects with frequent changes
- **Flexibility**: Maven's rigid lifecycle is easier to learn but harder to extend; Gradle's programmatic model handles complex scenarios naturally
- **Dependency management**: Both use transitive dependencies from Maven Central; Gradle adds features like dependency constraints and version catalogs
- **Enterprise adoption**: Maven dominates enterprise Java; Gradle is growing and standard for Android
- **Team expertise**: The tool your team knows well is usually the right choice — a poorly understood Gradle build is worse than a well-maintained Maven build
- **Migration path**: Gradle can consume Maven pom.xml files and dependencies, making gradual migration possible

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Maven and Gradle are both build tools, but they take different approaches. Maven uses XML for configuration — you declare what you want in a pom.xml file, and Maven follows a fixed lifecycle to build your project. It's convention-based, so every Maven project looks similar. Gradle uses a Groovy or Kotlin DSL, which means you write code to define your build. This makes Gradle way more flexible — you can express complex build logic that'd be painful in Maven's XML. The big practical difference is speed. Gradle has incremental builds, so it only recompiles files that changed. It also has a build cache that reuses outputs from previous builds, even across machines. In a large multi-module project, Gradle can be 10 to 100 times faster than Maven for incremental builds. That said, Maven's simpler and more familiar to most Java teams. If you're a fresher joining a project, you'll probably encounter Maven more often in enterprise settings. For a new project, I'd consider team expertise first — the tool your team knows is usually the right choice. If build speed matters and you've got Gradle skills on the team, Gradle's a strong pick. If predictability and wide compatibility matter more, Maven's safer.

questions.question: What are Gradle's incremental builds and build cache, and why do they matter?
questions.title: Gradle Incremental Builds and Build Cache
questions.direct_answer: Gradle's incremental builds skip recompiling files that haven't changed; the build cache goes further and reuses outputs from previous builds (even on other machines) when task inputs are identical — dramatically reducing build times.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of what makes Gradle faster — important when justifying Gradle adoption
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing incremental compilation with the build cache — they're related but different mechanisms
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that Gradle Enterprise's remote build cache lets CI and developer machines share cached build outputs

sections.title: How Gradle Achieves Faster Builds: Incremental Builds and Build Cache
sections.content:
Gradle's speed advantage comes from two complementary mechanisms. **Incremental builds** mean Gradle tracks which source files changed since the last build and only recompiles affected files — if you change one Java file, Gradle doesn't recompile the entire module.

Think of it like a chef preparing mise en place: you don't re-chop all the vegetables if you only need to add more onions. **The build cache** takes this further: Gradle computes a hash of each task's inputs (source files, dependencies, compiler flags) and stores the task's outputs in a cache. If you run a task with identical inputs later — even after a clean build or on a different machine — Gradle retrieves the cached outputs instead of re-executing the task. This is like having a pre-made sauce in the freezer: if the recipe hasn't changed, use the frozen one. Together, these features can reduce build times from minutes to seconds in large projects.

sections.title: Why Gradle Is Fast
sections.content:
amber|Incremental|~Only changed files|tracks inputs|skips unchanged|compiler-level smarts
blue|Build cache|~Reuse outputs|hashes task inputs|restores results|even after clean
emerald|Remote cache|~Share across machines|CI builds main|devs pull artifacts|Gradle Enterprise
violet|Two layers|~Not the same thing|incremental = javac|cache = Gradle tasks|they work together

sections.title: Enabling and Using the Build Cache
When These Features Matter Most
sections.content: **Incremental builds** shine during active development when you're making small changes and running builds frequently — if you change one controller, you don't want to wait for 50 other classes to recompile. The time savings scale with project size: in a 10-module project, incremental builds might save 10 seconds; in a 100-module project, they might save 2 minutes. **The build cache** is most valuable in two scenarios: (1) switching between Git branches — you checkout an old branch and Gradle reuses cached outputs from when you last built that branch, and (2) CI/CD pipelines with a **remote build cache** — multiple build agents share cached outputs, so PR builds reuse artifacts from the main branch build. Gradle Enterprise (paid product) provides a production-grade remote cache, but you can also set up a simple HTTP cache server.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Confusing incremental compilation with the build cache**: Freshers often think they're the same thing. Incremental compilation is Java-compiler-level (javac compiles only changed .java files); the build cache is Gradle-level (reuses entire task outputs like compiled classes, test results, or packaged JARs).
- **Not enabling the cache**: The build cache is opt-in via org.gradle.caching=true in gradle.properties. Many projects don't enable it and miss the benefits.
- **Cache-unfriendly tasks**: Custom Gradle tasks that don't declare inputs/outputs properly bypass the cache. If you write a task that reads files without telling Gradle, the cache won't work for that task.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Incremental builds**: Gradle tracks changed files and only recompiles what's necessary, not the entire project
- **Build cache**: Gradle stores task outputs (compiled classes, JARs, test results) indexed by input hashes and reuses them when inputs match
- **Local cache**: Stored in ~/.gradle/caches/build-cache-1/ and used automatically when org.gradle.caching=true
- **Remote cache**: Shared HTTP cache (Gradle Enterprise or custom) lets teams and CI share cached outputs across machines
- **Cache key**: Calculated from task inputs — source files, dependencies, compiler version, task configuration
- **Clean builds**: Even after ./gradlew clean, cached tasks can be restored from the cache, making "clean builds" nearly as fast as incremental ones
- **Performance impact**: In large multi-module projects, the combination can reduce build times from 10-15 minutes to under 1 minute

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Gradle's incremental builds and build cache are the two features that make it so much faster than Maven, especially in large projects. Incremental builds mean Gradle only recompiles files that changed. If you edit one Java file, Gradle doesn't rebuild the whole module — it just recompiles that file and anything that depends on it. That's a huge time saver during development. The build cache takes this further. Gradle hashes the inputs to every task — the source files, dependencies, compiler version, all of it — and stores the task's outputs in a cache. If you run the same task later with the same inputs, Gradle just pulls the outputs from the cache instead of re-running the task. This works even after a clean build. Say you do ./gradlew clean build, then do it again with no changes. The second time, Gradle retrieves everything from the cache and finishes in seconds instead of minutes. The really powerful part is the remote build cache. You can set up a shared cache server — Gradle Enterprise provides this — so your whole team and CI share cached outputs. If CI builds the main branch, developers can pull those cached artifacts when they build locally. One mistake freshers make is confusing these two features. Incremental compilation is the Java compiler being smart; the build cache is Gradle being smart. They're different layers, but they work together.

sections.title: Choosing Between Maven and Gradle: Context Over Dogma
sections.content:
The choice between Maven and Gradle isn't about which tool is objectively better — it's about **which tool fits your project, team, and constraints**. Maven is the safer, more conservative choice: it's been the Java build standard for 20 years, most enterprise developers know it, and its rigid conventions mean builds are predictable and maintainable.

Gradle is the performance-oriented, flexible choice: it handles complex build logic naturally, delivers significantly faster builds in large projects, and is the only option for Android. The biggest decision factor is often overlooked: **team expertise**. A Gradle build that no one on the team understands will become a maintenance nightmare, while a Maven build that everyone can modify will stay healthy. As a fresher, you'll likely inherit the choice rather than make it, but understanding the reasoning helps you contribute effectively.

emerald|Constraints|~Hard requirements|Android = Gradle only|corporate Maven standards|migration cost
violet|Default|~Lower risk|enterprise = Maven|complex builds = Gradle|context over dogma

sections.title: Maven pom.xml — Verbose, Familiar, Predictable
sections.content:
```xml
<project>
  <groupId>com.example</groupId>
  <artifactId>order-service</artifactId>
  <version>1.0.0</version>
  <dependencies>
    <dependency>
      <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
      <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
    </dependency>
  </dependencies>
</project>
```

sections.title: Gradle build.gradle — Concise, Flexible, Faster Rebuilds
Step 1: Evaluate Team Familiarity and Organizational Standards
sections.content: Start with your team's existing knowledge and your company's standards. **If your team is experienced with Maven** and your company has Maven archetypes, shared parent POMs, and established practices, switching to Gradle introduces risk without clear benefit — you'd spend weeks learning Gradle and migrating, time better spent building features. **If your organization has a Gradle mandate** (common in Android shops or companies that adopted Gradle early), use Gradle even if you're not familiar with it yet; you'll learn it on the job. **If you're a greenfield project with a mixed team**, lean toward Maven unless you have at least one strong Gradle expert who can mentor others. The maintenance burden of an unfamiliar build tool is real — obscure Gradle DSL errors are harder to debug than Maven's verbose-but-clear XML errors.

sections.title: Step 2: Consider Project Scale and Build Performance Requirements
sections.content: Project size and build frequency are the second major factor. **For small to medium projects** (1-5 modules, builds under 2 minutes), Maven and Gradle perform similarly, so team familiarity dominates the decision. **For large multi-module projects** (20+ modules, builds over 5 minutes), Gradle's incremental builds and build cache deliver measurable productivity gains — a 10-minute Maven build might become a 1-minute Gradle build after the first run. **If you're building for Android**, Gradle is mandatory; there's no choice to make. **If you need complex build orchestration** — code generation, multi-platform builds, custom workflows — Gradle's programmatic DSL handles this far more elegantly than Maven's plugin architecture. If your build is simple (compile, test, package), Maven's declarative XML is often clearer.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Choosing based on hype**: Freshers often say "Gradle is modern so I'd use Gradle" without considering that a tool is only as good as your team's ability to maintain it. A poorly understood Gradle build will accumulate technical debt faster than a well-maintained Maven build.
- **Ignoring the migration cost**: Switching from Maven to Gradle mid-project is expensive — you're not just converting pom.xml to build.gradle, you're retraining the team and updating CI/CD pipelines. Only do this if build performance is a genuine bottleneck.
- **Underestimating Maven's strengths**: Maven's rigidity is a feature, not a bug. Its conventions make it easy to onboard new developers and reason about builds. Don't dismiss this for flexibility you might not need.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Team expertise first**: The tool your team knows well is usually the right choice — a Gradle build no one understands is worse than a Maven build everyone can maintain
- **Project scale matters**: Small projects see little benefit from Gradle's speed; large multi-module projects see dramatic improvements
- **Organizational standards**: If your company has Maven archetypes and shared parent POMs, the switching cost is high
- **Android mandate**: Gradle is the only supported build tool for Android — no decision to make
- **Build complexity**: Gradle's programmatic DSL shines for custom workflows; Maven's XML is clearer for simple builds
- **Migration cost**: Converting a Maven project to Gradle is non-trivial — only do it if build performance is a real bottleneck
- **Default choice**: For enterprise Java projects with no special requirements, Maven is the safer, lower-risk default

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: I'd start by looking at the team and the organization's existing standards. If the team knows Maven well and the company has established Maven practices — shared parent POMs, archetypes, that kind of thing — I'd stick with Maven unless there's a really strong reason to switch. The risk of introducing a new tool that nobody fully understands usually outweighs the benefits, especially on a new project where you want to move fast. If the team already has Gradle expertise or the company's standardized on Gradle, then I'd use Gradle. The second factor is project scale. For small to medium projects, maybe up to five modules, Maven and Gradle perform about the same. The build time difference isn't significant enough to justify switching if your team knows Maven. But for large multi-module projects — say 20 or more modules — Gradle's incremental builds and build cache can cut build times dramatically, like from 10 minutes down to one or two minutes. That's a real productivity gain. For Android development, there's no choice — you have to use Gradle. If you're building a standard Spring Boot microservice with a straightforward build, Maven's simpler. Its XML is verbose but clear, and everyone knows how to read it. If you need complex build logic — code generation, custom workflows, integrating non-Java tools — Gradle's Groovy DSL handles that way better than Maven's plugin system. The key point is there's no universal right answer. It's context-dependent. Team familiarity is usually the most important factor.

questions.title: Gradle build.gradle for Spring Boot
questions.direct_answer: A basic Spring Boot build.gradle has plugins (java + spring-boot + dependency-management), repositories (mavenCentral()), dependencies declared with implementation/testImplementation, and the java block for version settings.

sections.title: Anatomy of a Spring Boot Gradle Build File
sections.content:
A **build.gradle** file for Spring Boot follows a structured pattern: plugins at the top, Java version configuration, dependency repositories, and then the dependencies themselves.

Think of it like a recipe: first you declare what tools you're using (plugins), then set up where ingredients come from (repositories), then list the ingredients (dependencies). The **plugins block** applies the Java plugin (for compiling Java code), the Spring Boot plugin (for packaging as an executable JAR), and the dependency management plugin (for inheriting Spring Boot's dependency versions). The **repositories block** tells Gradle where to download dependencies from — almost always mavenCentral(). The **dependencies block** lists libraries using configurations like **implementation** (compile-time and runtime dependency) or **testImplementation** (test-only dependency). Unlike Maven's pom.xml, Gradle's build.gradle is executable code, so you can use variables, conditionals, and loops if needed.

sections.title: Minimal Spring Boot build.gradle
When You'll Encounter and Modify This File
sections.content: You'll work with **build.gradle** whenever you add a new dependency (a library like Jackson, Lombok, or a database driver), change the Java version, or configure build behavior. The most common task for freshers is **adding dependencies**: open build.gradle, add a line like implementation 'com.fasterxml.jackson.core:jackson-databind:2.16.0' in the dependencies block, and run ./gradlew build. Gradle downloads the library and makes it available to your code. You'll also modify this file to **configure plugins** — for example, adding the Lombok plugin or configuring the bootJar task to set the main class. Unlike Maven's pom.xml, which is declarative, Gradle's build.gradle is imperative, so you can write Groovy code to compute values or conditionally include dependencies based on environment variables.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using 'compile' instead of 'implementation'**: Older Gradle tutorials use the deprecated 'compile' configuration. In modern Gradle, use 'implementation' for dependencies that are both compile-time and runtime.
- **Forgetting 'testImplementation'**: Freshers often add test libraries (like JUnit, Mockito) with 'implementation', making them available in production code, which bloats the final JAR. Use 'testImplementation' for test-only dependencies.
- **Not understanding 'api' vs 'implementation'**: In multi-module projects, 'implementation' hides transitive dependencies from consumers, while 'api' exposes them. Most single-module projects only need 'implementation', but if you're writing a library module, understanding this distinction matters.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **plugins block**: Declares build plugins — 'java', 'org.springframework.boot', and 'io.spring.dependency-management' are typical for Spring Boot
- **java block**: Sets sourceCompatibility (Java version for source code) and optionally targetCompatibility (JVM bytecode version)
- **repositories**: mavenCentral() tells Gradle to download dependencies from Maven Central Repository
- **implementation**: Gradle configuration for dependencies needed at compile-time and runtime (equivalent to Maven's 'compile' scope)
- **testImplementation**: For test-only dependencies like JUnit and Mockito — not included in the production JAR
- **runtimeOnly**: For dependencies only needed at runtime (like JDBC drivers) — not on the compile classpath
- **api vs implementation**: In multi-module projects, 'api' exposes transitive dependencies to consumers; 'implementation' hides them for faster builds

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: A basic Gradle build file for Spring Boot starts with the plugins block. You apply three plugins: the java plugin to compile Java code, the spring-boot plugin to package your app as an executable JAR, and the dependency-management plugin to inherit Spring Boot's dependency versions. Next, you set the Java version in the java block using sourceCompatibility. For Spring Boot 3, that's usually Java 17 or later. Then you have the repositories block, which almost always just says mavenCentral(). That tells Gradle where to download dependencies from. The dependencies block is where you list your libraries. You use 'implementation' for dependencies you need at compile-time and runtime, like spring-boot-starter-web or spring-boot-starter-data-jpa. You use 'testImplementation' for test-only stuff like JUnit or Mockito. There's also 'runtimeOnly' for things you only need at runtime, like database drivers. One thing to note: 'implementation' in Gradle is like 'compile' scope in Maven. Older Gradle code used 'compile', but that's deprecated now. A common mistake is using 'implementation' for test dependencies instead of 'testImplementation', which means your test libraries get bundled into the production JAR unnecessarily. If you're building a library that other modules depend on, you'd also learn about 'api' versus 'implementation'. The 'api' configuration exposes transitive dependencies to consumers, while 'implementation' hides them. That helps with build performance in large projects.
